text: Chinchilla's correction to earlier scaling guidance hinged on one detail: the learning-rate schedule actually matching the run. At real pretraining scale, getting this schedule wrong doesn't just slow convergence down, it can blow up the entire run.

At initialization, weights are random and the optimizer's internal moment estimates haven't settled yet. A large learning rate from step zero can push weights straight out of a stable region. The fix is linear warmup: ramp the rate from near zero up to its target peak over the first few hundred to few thousand steps.

Once warmup ends, the rate needs to come back down for the rest of training — almost always along a cosine curve from peak to some small minimum. In practice nobody hand-rolls this: Hugging Face's get_cosine_schedule_with_warmup wraps a PyTorch optimizer directly, and you just call scheduler.step() alongside optimizer.step() every training step.

Peak learning rate itself is chosen relative to model size — bigger models generally use smaller peak rates, often informed by small-scale sweeps extrapolated the same way scaling laws are. Cosine decay is the most common shape, though warmup-stable-decay, which holds a constant rate and only decays near the end, is gaining ground for runs with a flexible token budget.

A peak rate that's too high is one of the most common root causes of the loss spikes we cover next — so treat warmup and a conservative peak as a stability measure, not just a speed tweak. Up next: loss spikes and training instability.
